1226575764751028225 [2020-02-09] @DRMacIver 💜 38 🔁 3 [(SEED) type=semantic_search]
Every piece of advice that you think everybody needs is literally the worst possible advice you could give at least one person.
↓
1226575984989810690 [2020-02-09] @DRMacIver 💜 15
Typically this is because they've already internalised an unhealthily strong version of that advice.

The point of advice is to push people in the direction of optimum, and you'll almost never find a situation where optimum is the same direction for everybody.
↓
1226577100842381314 [2020-02-09] @DRMacIver 💜 22 🔁 3
e.g. "Think about whether you're the asshole in this situation" is broadly good advice to most people, but really not good advice to someone with enough social anxiety that they could write an 8000 word essay about why they're definitely the asshole in every situation they're in.

  - [Image #0] The image shows a passage of text. The text is as follows:
    
    "This is how it should be done. Lodge yourself on a stratum, experiment with the opportunities it offers, find an advantageous place on it, find potential movements of deterritorialization, possible lines of flight, experience them, produce flow conjunctions here and there, try out continua of intensities segment by segment, have a small plot of new land at all times. It is through a meticulous relation with the strata that one succeeds in freeing lines of flight, causing conjugated flows to pass and escape and bringing forth continuous intensities for a BwO. (Deleuze & Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus, 1980/1987, p. 161)"

rating.reasoning_summary: This strand centers on the paradox of advice-giving itself: the recognition that all advice is contextual, often misapplied, and that the most transformative guidance sounds 'stupid as hell' when verbalized. Beginning with DRMacIver's 2020 observation that universal advice is impossible (everyone's optimum differs), the discourse crystallizes around bashu_thanks' viral 2023 tweet about soul-guiding advice that cannot be shared. The community then demonstrates this principle by sharing their own 'stupid-sounding' mantras (NVC's thank-you/please, hokey pokey wisdom, 'be like cat'), creating a meta-commentary on the limits of linguistic transmission. This is primarily a dialectical strand—people are wrestling with the tension between wanting to help others and recognizing advice as a lossy compression of lived experience. The boundary object is the ineffability of transformative knowledge itself.

title: The best advice sounds dumb out loud
summary:
The killer take came from @bashu_thanks: everyone has “one piece of advice… that guides the movement of their soul,” but it “sounds stupid as hell” so you can’t say it. Then he immediately proves it with his own supposedly-cringe mantra from Marshall Rosenberg (NVC): “Everybody’s always either saying thank you or please and if you don’t hear a thank you it’s a please.” He swears it rewired how he understands humans, but when he quotes it people act like he’s high—because the whole point is that transformative advice is basically un-transmittable unless it slots into your brain at the right moment.

That tweet detonates a meta-thread where everyone reenacts the same phenomenon. @visakanv says the deepest truths are “encoded in children songs like the hokey pokey and row your boat,” i.e., stuff that sounds like nursery nonsense until it hits you (“life is but a dream”). @ElodesNL drops the gut-punch version: “whatever you think the world has been withholding from you, you have been withholding from the world,” and people reply like they’ve been physically struck. @DRMacIver—who planted the earlier philosophical landmine back in 2020 (“Every piece of advice that you think everybody needs is literally the worst possible advice you could give at least one person”)—adds his own ultra-compressed koan: “everything is the same as everything else,” with the caveat that the “one topic” is huge. Meanwhile the thread’s jokier edge keeps it honest: @AskYatharth offers “be like cat,” and @imperialauditor contributes “finite problems, bitch,” like a bumper-sticker version of epistemic humility.

The arc is basically: (1) years of people warning that advice is context-dependent and often harmful when misapplied (@DRMacIver’s “optimum differs,” the social-anxiety “are you the asshole?” counterexample), (2) bashu’s viral October 2023 moment that turns it into a meme-able confession—your real guiding principle is embarrassingly simple, (3) peak synthesis in 2024 when @visakanv posts the “finger pointing at the moon” comic: instructions get turned into idols, and then everyone argues about whether misunderstanding still helps (e.g., @sunriseoath’s “fail upward”). It kind of dies by looping back into itself: advice about advice, and finally @dwarkesh_sp lands the cleanest meta-advice of all—writing advice that works because it bypasses the mystical packaging: “What are you trying to say here? Okay, just write that.”

Why care: because this explains why “obvious” guidance (therapy slogans, spiritual pointers, productivity tips) either changes your life or bounces off like noise—and why your most important beliefs often sound like fortune cookies until you’ve lived the footnotes.
